exactBefore.body:
## Chef's Note

Congealed salads are a Southern tradition - aspic-based dishes that served as both side dish and dessert at mid-century dinners. Despite their reputation, they work because the gelatin provides a light texture that carries fruit and nuts without heaviness. The trick is chilling just until set but not rock-hard, so each spoonful has a slight wobble.

## Directions

1.  **Dissolve:** In a large bowl, whisk the Jello into the boiling water until no crystals remain.
2.  **Combine:** Stir in the thawed strawberries, drained pineapple, and mashed bananas. Fold in the pecans if using.
3.  **Stage 1:** Pour exactly half of the mixture into a 9x13 glass dish. **Refrigerate for 1-2 hours** until firm. Keep the remaining half at room temperature.
4.  **The Emulsion:** Once the first layer is set, spread the sour cream in an even layer over the top.
5.  **Stage 2:** Carefully pour the remaining Jello mixture over the sour cream.
6.  **Set:** Return to the fridge for **at least 2 more hours** (ideally 4) until completely congealed.
7.  **Serve:** Slice into squares and serve cold.

frontmatter.title: Strawberry Congealed Salad
ingredients: 1 package (6 oz) regular strawberry gelatin dessert mix
2 packages (10 oz) frozen strawberries, thawed in the refrigerator and drained; discard the released liquid
1 can (20 oz) canned crushed pineapple, drained; discard the packing liquid
water for an external warm-water bath, warm, not boiling; only if the refrigerated reserved mixture needs gently reliquefying; do not add it to the salad, optional
equipment: 9×13-inch dish at least 2 inches deep, about 3-quart capacity

learning.focus: Build two fruit-gelatin layers around a full sour-cream layer while keeping the reserved half cold.
learning.outcome: Rich chilled strawberry, pineapple and banana layers with sour cream and optional pecan crunch.
before: Use regular strawberry gelatin dessert mix at the displayed weight; sugar-free mix is not interchangeable by package count.
Thaw the strawberries in the refrigerator and drain both fruits well. Use canned pineapple, not raw pineapple.
Prepare cold space for the whole dish and the entire reserved half. For larger quantities, use separate complete dishes with similar shallow layer depths; dimensions and chill times do not multiply.

checkpoints.cue: No dry gelatin grains remain and the base is still fluid.
checkpoints.why: Complete dissolution matters before the chilled fruit is added.

checkpoints.cue: The first layer is firm enough to support sour cream; the covered second half is refrigerated.
checkpoints.why: A cold reserve controls perishable holding while the first layer sets.

checkpoints.cue: Reserved gelatin is fluid but no longer warm to the touch before it touches the cold cream.
checkpoints.why: Gentle remelting restores pourability; a hot top layer can disturb the set bottom and cream.

checkpoints.cue: The chilled upper layer has no freely moving liquid and the center supports a portion.
checkpoints.why: Layer depth and fruit moisture affect the final setting time.

troubleshooting.problem: The reserved second half has set.
troubleshooting.cause: It was held safely cold while the first layer firmed.
troubleshooting.fix: Gently reliquefy it in an external warm-water bath without adding liquid, then cool it just until no longer warm while still pourable before layering.

troubleshooting.problem: The sour-cream layer mixes into the gelatin.
troubleshooting.cause: The bottom was not firm enough, or the upper mixture was hot or poured forcefully.
troubleshooting.fix: Wait for a supported bottom layer, keep the sour cream cold, and spoon the no-longer-warm upper mixture gently over it.

troubleshooting.problem: The salad remains loose after the planning clock.
troubleshooting.cause: The dish is deep, fruit drainage differs, or the gelatin product changed.
troubleshooting.fix: Continue chilling and follow the center cue. Use the specified regular gelatin and drained fruit for the next batch.

substitutions.alternative: For the banana-forward version, use large bananas in place of the displayed medium bananas and half the displayed pecan amount; all other quantities and the complete method stay the same
substitutions.effect: More banana and less nut crunch. The full sour-cream layer and both complete fruit layers remain.

learning.timing: The listed batch plans twelve side or dessert portions, without a measured finished volume. Allow about 25–35 minutes active work split between mixing and final layering, roughly 1–2 hours or longer for the first set, then at least 4 hours or overnight for the final set. Plan 6–8 hours or overnight overall, continuing to the center cues. Keep the reserved half refrigerated between stages; a gentle remelt is a brief handling step, not a new multi-hour counter hold. Fractional banana quantities should be mashed and divided proportionally rather than rounded up or down.
learning.storage: Keep covered at 40°F / 4°C or below and use within 3–4 days of preparation, following any earlier deadline from the sour cream or thawed fruit. Keep total preparation and serving time out of refrigeration within 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90°F / 32°C; use ice or an insulated cooler to maintain cold holding at a gathering. Do not freeze to speed setting; freezing can damage the gel texture. Keep the reserved uncooked mixture refrigerated between layers; later warming does not reset its storage deadline.

exactAfter.body:
## Chef's Note

This Southern congealed salad keeps two strawberry-fruit layers around a full sour-cream layer. Drained strawberries and pineapple bring bright fruit, mashed bananas give body, and the optional full pecan amount adds crunch. Let the first layer support the cream before finishing the top, and keep the reserved fruit mixture refrigerated between stages.

## Directions

1. **Prepare the dish and fruit:** Make refrigerator space for a 9×13-inch dish at least 2 inches deep with about 3-quart capacity and a covered heatproof bowl for the reserved mixture. Clean the pineapple can lid before opening. Drain frozen strawberries and canned crushed pineapple well, discarding their free liquid; peel and mash medium banana. Keep the fruit and sour cream cold until needed.
2. **Dissolve the gelatin completely:** Put regular strawberry gelatin dessert mix and boiling water in a heatproof bowl. Stir about 2 minutes and continue until all dry grains dissolve. This concentrated family mixture uses the listed boiling water only; do not add the plain-package cold-water amount. Let it lose its steaming heat while it remains fluid.
3. **Combine the complete fruit mixture:** Fold in frozen strawberries, canned crushed pineapple, medium bananas, and pecans (if using), including the full chopped pecan amount if using. Stir until the fruit is evenly distributed. All of this mixture is used across the two gelatin layers.
4. **Chill both halves:** Divide the complete fruit-gelatin mixture into two equal halves, stirring between transfers so the fruit and nuts are shared evenly. Spread one half in the prepared dish, cover, and refrigerate at 40°F / 4°C or below. Cover the entire reserved second half in its separate heatproof bowl and refrigerate it too. Begin checking the first layer around 1–2 hours, continuing until it is firm enough to support the sour-cream layer without flowing.
5. **Add all the sour cream:** Once the bottom layer is firm, spread full-fat sour cream gently and evenly over it, keeping the sour cream in a distinct layer. Return the dish to refrigeration while preparing the reserved mixture.
6. **Keep the reserved half pourable and add it:** Take the reserved mixture from the refrigerator. If it has set, place its bowl in water for an external warm-water bath (if using) and stir gently just until the gelatin becomes pourable; keep bath water out of the bowl and do not boil the mixture. Remove from the bath and let it become no longer warm to the touch while still pourable. Stir to redistribute fruit, then spoon or pour all of it gently over the cold sour-cream layer. If it is already fluid, use it directly. Keep total preparation time out of refrigeration within 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90°F / 32°C.
7. **Finish setting and serve cold:** Cover and refrigerate promptly. Allow at least 4 more hours or overnight, continuing until the upper layer holds a gentle jiggle without freely flowing liquid and the center supports a cut or spooned portion. Keep refrigerated until serving.

## Cooking Notes

Use canned pineapple and drained fruit as listed. Keep all of the sour cream in the middle layer. For the banana-forward version, use large bananas instead of the displayed medium bananas and half the displayed pecan amount; keep everything else the same. Divide the finished fruit-gelatin mixture equally so both layers receive their share of fruit and nuts.

sourceDifferences: Manufacturer plain 6-oz gelatin would use a different water schedule; this concentrated family formula retains 1 cup boiling water and no cold-water addition, with fruit supplying additional moisture. Do not silently normalize it to plain gelatin.

GME warns against boiling already hydrated gelatin; manufacturer commercial Jell-O explicitly calls for initial boiling water. Follow the product’s initial dissolution instruction and use only gentle heat for the later reserve remelt.
The native gives two 10-oz frozen strawberry packages, medium bananas and a full optional cup of pecans; current changed banana size/nuts are preserved as a distinct adapted option.
The original sets each layer1–2 hours with no explicit reserve holding instruction; current room-temperature holding was added later and is replaced for safe handling.
